opus-5.5.text:
I think "emergence" is a word people use a bit loosely, so let me separate a few meanings.

The first is the measurement sense. You plot performance on some task against model scale, and for a long time it looks flat, near random. Then past a certain size it jumps. People called that emergence. Some of that turns out to be an artifact of the metric. If you only score exact-match answers, a model that is getting closer and closer looks like it's at zero until it suddenly isn't. With a smoother metric, like log-likelihood of the right answer, the curve often looks much more continuous. So part of the "magic" is just how we chose to look.

But I don't think that explains it all away, and that's the second, deeper sense. The training objective is extremely simple: predict the next token. Nobody wrote a module for arithmetic, translation, coding, or theory of mind. Yet to predict text written by humans really well, you end up needing compressed internal models of a lot of the processes that generated that text: grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, even how people think about other people. Capabilities you never specified fall out of a simple objective applied at enough scale to rich enough data. That's emergence in the more physics-like sense: simple local rules, complex global behavior.

The third sense is about composition. Once a model has a bunch of basic skills, it can combine them in ways that weren't in the training data. In-context learning is a good example. You show a few examples in the prompt and the model picks up a new task without any weight update. Nobody trained that explicitly. It came from the structure of the data plus scale. And when you add things like chain-of-thought or reinforcement learning on reasoning, abilities that were latent become usable. So a lot of what looks like emergence is really latent capability being unlocked by the right interface or the right post-training.

My overall view is that it's less mysterious than the word suggests, but more profound than the skeptics allow. It's not that intelligence appears from nothing at some critical parameter count. Pretraining on human-generated data gives you an enormous prior, a compressed version of a lot of human knowledge and thinking. What we call emergence is the moment that prior becomes rich and coherent enough that you can steer it toward general problem solving.

The interesting open question for me is what comes next. If the first wave of emergence came from imitating human data, the next wave probably has to come from interaction: models acting, getting feedback, and learning from their own experience, not just from what humans already wrote down. Whether genuinely new capabilities emerge from that loop, beyond the human prior, is what I find most exciting right now.

r001.rationale: The response says some apparent emergence comes from metric choices and latent capabilities being unlocked, but it also describes a deeper, real emergence of complex capabilities from scale and data. It does not characterize emergence overall as mainly subjective rather than objective.

r002.rationale: The response links capabilities to scale, rich data, and post-training, but does not identify a technological change that enables scaling to improve capabilities broadly.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "emergence" is a word people use when they don't yet have a good explanation, and that's fine, but I try not to let it do too much work.

The way I'd put it is this. You take a model and give it one very simple objective: predict the next token. There is nothing in that objective that says "learn to reason" or "learn to code" or "learn to write a plan." But to predict the next token well on human text, the cheapest path, in terms of compression, is often to actually model the process that generated the text. If a mathematician wrote the proof, the easiest way to predict the next line is to partially become the thing that produces proofs. So intelligence isn't the goal of the training, it's a byproduct of the goal being hard enough and the data being rich enough.

When I was doing the ReAct and Tree of Thoughts work, the thing that struck me was that these behaviors were already sitting inside the model. We didn't train reasoning in. We just gave the model a format where it could externalize its thinking, let it act in an environment and see the result, and suddenly tasks that looked impossible became doable. So part of what people call emergence is really just the gap between what a model can do and what we've figured out how to elicit from it. The capability was latent, and the interface was the bottleneck.

The second thing I'd say is that emergence is often an artifact of how we measure. If you use a metric like exact match, a model that is 40 percent of the way to a right answer scores zero, and then at some scale it crosses a threshold and the curve jumps. If you look at log-likelihood instead, it's usually smooth. So a lot of the "sudden" feeling is the discontinuity of our evaluation, not of the model.

But I don't want to be too deflationary, because there is something real here. Language is special. It's not just one modality among many. It's the medium humans use to think, to coordinate, to pass down abstractions. So a model trained on language inherits a huge amount of structure about how to decompose problems, how to recall, how to plan. That's why I've argued that the right way to think about language models now is less as text generators and more as a kind of general-purpose reasoning and acting engine, where language is the internal representation for thought.

And the piece I'm most interested in going forward is this: pre-training gives you priors, but the real leap in intelligence comes when you close the loop with an environment. A model that can act, observe, and update is in a fundamentally different regime than one that just predicts. That's where I think the next phase of "emergence" will come from, and it won't look like a surprise on a benchmark. It'll look like systems that get better at tasks by doing them.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation can make progress look sudden and describes some capabilities as latent, but it also says there is something real about emergence and does not characterize it overall as more subjective impression than objective phenomenon.

r002.rationale: It identifies acting, observing, and updating through an environment as a shift toward a different regime, but does not say this technological change enables scaling to improve capabilities broadly.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is how a model trained to predict the next token can acquire abilities that look like reasoning or problem-solving. The other is why some of those abilities seem to appear suddenly as models get larger. They’re related, but they’re not the same question.

For the first, predicting language is a simple objective, but doing it well isn’t necessarily a simple task. Language contains descriptions of the world, people’s intentions, and the steps involved in solving problems. A model can improve prediction by learning some of those underlying structures. So the training objective doesn’t have to explicitly say “learn to reason” for reasoning-like behavior to become useful.

For the second, I would be careful about the word “suddenly.” Suppose you evaluate a task where an answer is either completely correct or completely wrong. The model might be improving gradually, but your metric only registers that improvement once it crosses a threshold. That can make a continuous change look like a sudden emergence. Other cases might involve a more substantial change in how the model solves the task, but observing a jump in accuracy alone doesn’t establish that.

What interests me most is whether an ability is reliable and generalizable. Can the model use it on an unfamiliar problem? Can it recover after making a mistake? Can it interact with an environment and check whether its answer works? Those questions help us move from saying “this looks intelligent” to understanding what the system can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response says apparent suddenness can result from threshold-based evaluation and that an accuracy jump alone proves little. It does not characterize emergence itself as more subjective than objective.

r002.rationale: The response discusses gradual improvement and evaluation, but does not identify a technological change that enables scaling to improve capabilities broadly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we first need to distinguish two meanings of emergence. One is that a model becomes more capable as you increase its scale. The other is that a capability seems to appear suddenly: smaller models cannot do something, and then a larger model can.

The second is interesting, but we have to be careful about how we measure it. Suppose a task requires ten steps, and we only count an answer as correct if all ten succeed. Each individual step might improve gradually, while the overall success rate looks like a sudden jump. So an apparent discontinuity in intelligence can sometimes come from the evaluation metric.

But there is still a deeper question: why does predicting the next token produce capabilities that seem to go beyond text prediction? My intuition is that language contains traces of the processes that generate it—reasoning, knowledge, interaction with the world. To predict language well across many situations, a model benefits from learning some of that underlying structure.

I wouldn’t say that this automatically explains intelligence, though. For me, the important question is whether those capabilities remain reliable when you change the problem, and whether a model can use them to act, receive feedback, and solve tasks over time. Emergence is an observation that needs an explanation, rather than an explanation by itself.

r001.rationale: The candidate says apparent jumps can result from evaluation metrics and calls emergence an observation needing explanation, but does not characterize emergence overall as more subjective than objective.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions capabilities increasing with scale, but does not identify a technological change as the qualitative boundary that enables broad capability improvements through scaling.
